title: Hosanna in the temple (Matthew 21:1–17)
hook: children shout hosanna in the temple; the leaders object; he quotes a psalm
carry: out of the mouths of babes
tomorrow: two sons: one says yes, one says no. which one did the father's will?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two blind men who cried the more, and a plain ask: that our eyes may be opened. They followed him up the road. Today the road reaches Jerusalem.
screen: `THAT OUR EYES MAY BE OPENED.` → `THE ROAD REACHES JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: A toddler shouts the last line of a song a beat too late, in the quiet part, and heads turn. Some people smile. Some wince. Matthew has a scene like that. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, and the crowds cry, "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest." In the temple he overturns the moneychangers' tables, and the blind and the lame come to him there, and he heals them. And then the children pick up the crowd's words and start shouting them, right in the temple: Hosanna to the son of David.
screen: `A SHOUT IN THE QUIET PART.` → `A KING ON A DONKEY.` → `CHILDREN SHOUTING IN THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: The chief priests and scribes are sore displeased. "Hearest thou what these say?" And here is the answer to yesterday's question. Jesus quotes their own scripture back: "Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?" That line is from Psalm eight. The leaders heard noise. He heard praise. Now a question Christians still argue over, kindly: where do children belong in worship? Some churches keep children in the whole service. Their case: this very scene. The children were in the temple, loud, and he defended them. Faith is learned by being in the room, wiggles and all, and a church that sends its kids out may be telling them the real thing is for adults. Other churches hold children's worship for part of the service. Their case is strong too: kids praise more fully with songs and words made for them, at their pace, and parents get a few quiet minutes to listen. Jesus' line, they'd say, is about praise, not about the seating chart. Hear what both sides already agree on. Neither calls a child's praise noise. The argument is about how best to make room for it.
screen: `HEAREST THOU WHAT THESE SAY?` · `OUT OF THE MOUTH OF BABES.` · `KEEP THEM IN THE ROOM.` · `GIVE THEM THEIR OWN ROOM.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE MOUTHS OF BABES.`

segments.voice: For the sit, listen for the smallest live sound you can hear: a kid outside, a bird, a neighbor's radio, the hum of the building. Don't judge it as noise or music; let it be part of the room, the way the children's shouting was part of the temple.
Hosanna in the temple. The children's shout that the leaders wanted stopped, and Jesus called praise.
Pocket this one: out of the mouths of babes, praise made perfect. That's the day.

howItsDone: On Palm Sunday some churches hand out palms and some have children lead the procession; churches differ on whether children stay for the whole service or have their own worship for part of it.

fork.setup: your church is debating moving kids to their own worship time. you want them to stay in the main service. what's the other side's best case?

fork.reveal: the strongest case for children's worship is about making room for their praise, not shushing it. both sides agree with Jesus: a child's praise is not noise.

notes: Debate shape: children in the whole service vs. children's worship for part of it. Both cases are given at their best and neither is assigned to a named denomination. Confirm fairness.

Hosanna: the gloss avoids the etymology (often given as Hebrew 'save, we pray', Psalm 118:25) under the claims rule; a Keeper may add it. Matthew's Psalm 8:2 wording ('perfected praise') differs from the KJV Psalm ('ordained strength'); not raised in the voice.
The temple action (21:12–13) is mentioned in one clause; the 'den of thieves' quotation from the older draft is cut for length.
